repos.title: Watch Your Step: Anticipated Perception for Humanoid Locomotion
repos.paper_summary: Watch Your Step introduces a perceptive locomotion framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid in which a lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts the next two footholds from proprioception and the velocity command, and the policy observes only small 7×7 elevation-map patches around those predicted footholds. The FPM is an MLP with two 128-unit hidden layers, trained by Huber regression on labeled footholds from recent policy rollouts and refit every 500 PPO iterations, jointly with a PPO locomotion policy. On the training terrain curriculum, the FPM policy reaches level 5 after 7.5k iterations, against 26.1k for the complete-map baseline (HM) and 20.0k for an attention-based encoder (AME2). AME2 ends slightly higher at 40k iterations but needs four GPUs and 6.3 s per policy update versus 0.55 s. In simulation, the FPM policy achieves 74.2% success on sparse corridor terrain versus 71.7% for AME2 and at most 42.7% for the other baselines, and 77.7% on out-of-distribution gaps. The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 on stairs, a 0.55 m gap, and a 0.6 m drop. Limitations include reliance on an elevation map and that the policy's cautious behavior near unseen gaps is a hypothesis rather than a measured result.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Predicting footholds from proprioception and filtering the elevation map around them should cut redundant input for perceptive humanoid locomotion.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: The locomotion task is set as a reinforcement learning problem for a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid trained with PPO in 8192 parallel environments.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A blind foothold predictor is retrained periodically, and the policy sees only small height patches around its two predicted footholds.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments and Results
digest_headlines.headline: The gated policy reaches curriculum level 5 in 7.5k iterations, 3.4 to 3.5 times faster than full-map methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The approach trails full-map methods on stepped corridor terrain and cannot see obstacles approaching from the side.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Sampling the elevation map around predicted footholds learns faster than full-map policies and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1.

repos.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
repos.paper_summary:
Graph RAG is a method for answering global questions over large text corpora by using an LLM to build an entity knowledge graph and pre-generate hierarchical community summaries. The pipeline extracts entities and relationships from source text chunks, partitions the resulting graph into communities using the Leiden algorithm, and summarizes each community. At query time, it generates partial answers from community summaries in parallel and synthesizes them into a final response. This differs from standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which retrieves local text chunks and fails on corpus-wide sensemaking questions.

The authors evaluated Graph RAG against naïve RAG and a map-reduce baseline that summarizes raw source texts directly. They used two datasets of approximately 1 million tokens and 125 LLM-generated sensemaking questions per dataset. An LLM-as-a-judge assessed answers on comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and directness. Global approaches outperformed naïve RAG, with comprehensiveness win rates between 72% and 83%. Intermediate-level community summaries provided better comprehensiveness and diversity than source-text summarization while using 26–33% fewer context tokens. Root-level summaries reduced token usage by over 97% compared to source-text processing. Limitations include evaluation on only two specific datasets and question types, with no validation of fabrication rates or end-user utility.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RAG cannot answer corpus-wide sensemaking questions, so GraphRAG builds an entity graph with community summaries and outperforms vector RAG with GPT-4.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers graph-based retrieval, hierarchical summaries and benchmarks oriented toward explicit fact retrieval rather than global questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: GraphRAG extracts an entity graph, detects Leiden communities, summarizes them, and answers queries by map-reduce over summaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments compare six conditions on two corpora of about one million tokens, using generated global sensemaking questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Global GraphRAG conditions beat vector RAG on comprehensiveness at 72-83% win rates on podcast transcripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation covers only two corpora and lacks a fabrication-rate comparison, which the authors name as limitations.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Root-level community summaries give a data index that beats vector RAG and competes with other global methods at lower token cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extraction prompts, self-reflection gleaning, community detection, context window tests, an example comparison, and system prompts.

repos.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
repos.paper_summary: The Switch Transformer replaces the standard feed-forward layer in Transformers with a sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) module that routes each token to a single expert, reducing communication overhead and improving training stability. By using top-1 routing instead of top-k, the model maintains constant computational cost per token while scaling parameter count. The paper introduces selective precision casting to stabilize bfloat16 training and an auxiliary load-balancing loss to ensure uniform expert usage. Experiments on the C4 corpus show that a 64-expert Switch-Base model achieves the same pre-training quality as T5-Base in one-seventh the time. Fine-tuning results indicate consistent improvements over T5-Base and T5-Large on GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, and summarization tasks. Distilling these sparse models into dense T5-Base architectures preserves approximately 30% of the quality gain while compressing model size by up to 99%. In multilingual settings across 101 languages, the method yields a mean 5x speedup over mT5-Base. A limitation is that distillation does not fully recover teacher performance, and the approach relies on specific hardware parallelism strategies for trillion-parameter scales.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse expert routing is proposed to add parameters without raising per-example compute, with gains across pre-training, fine-tuning and multilingual training.

digest_headlines.heading: Switch Transformer
digest_headlines.headline: Routing each token to one expert simplifies Mixture of Experts, with capacity limits and a balancing loss keeping training stable.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Properties
digest_headlines.headline: Increasing experts at fixed FLOPS per token speeds up pre-training, with Switch-Base 64 reaching T5-Base quality in one-seventh the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Downstream Results
digest_headlines.headline: Switch models improve most T5 fine-tuning tasks, distill to dense models keeping 30% of gains, and beat mT5 on all 101 languages.

digest_headlines.heading: Designing Models with Data, Model, and Expert-Parallelism
digest_headlines.headline: Data, model and expert parallelism combine to train 395 billion and 1.6 trillion parameter Switch models, with Switch-XXL sometimes unstable.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work scales models through model parallelism and conditional computation, including mixture of experts and attention sparsity.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse models are argued to outperform dense models per step and on wall clock time, but distilled versions keep only about 30% of gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Remaining challenges include stabilizing the largest models, heterogeneous experts, expert layers beyond feed-forward layers, and other modalities.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Switch Transformers are presented as stable, sample-efficient language learners across pre-training, fine-tuning and multi-task training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers attention Switch layers, token rerouting, router exploration, small-scale results, upstream-downstream correlation and pseudocode.

repos.title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
repos.paper_summary: AIPOCH Open-Science is an open-source AI research workbench that exports and imports research sessions as portable `.science` packages. The package keeps recorded relations among task context, executed activities, artifact versions, reviews and retained files, and it maps identifiers to the receiving workspace. The authors specify this exchange contract and test it on one controlled session with an incorrect first output, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted permutation test. Complete and partial exports were compared with source snapshots extracted independently of the exporter, and both imports into separate projects retained the tested version and review associations. The unreviewed revision stayed distinct from earlier assessments, and excluded content was marked unavailable. A separate registry case linked a table to its recorded task, execution and review. Offline re-execution of its retained script on a fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. Limitations stated by the paper include that the controlled test used one session and one installation, that native input-edge rows were absent, and that initial task attribution still depends on the surrounding conversation.

digest_headlines.heading: Author affiliations
digest_headlines.headline: The author list spans many hospitals and companies, mainly in China, with affiliations also in the Netherlands, Israel and the United States.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sharing AI-assisted research needs its task, version and review relations to survive transfer, not only the output files.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier provenance and session-sharing systems cover parts of the problem; this work focuses on version and review attribution after exchange.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods and implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The method maps workbench records into typed objects and relations, then checks an exported package against an independently extracted source reference.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Relations, not just files, survived export in a controlled session, with all paired comparisons matching in both exchange conditions.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: A failed assessment, its correction and an unreviewed revision can all be true together, so exchange must keep each target separate.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The contract keeps recorded version and review relations across identifier mapping and explicit omissions, with evidence limited to the tested records.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and code availability
digest_headlines.headline: The software is released under Apache 2.0, and a de-identified validation release on Hugging Face contains the protocol, packages and audit scripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of AI assistance
digest_headlines.headline: Codex assisted with literature retrieval, source inspection, application operation and validation code, and the authors remain responsible for interpretation.

digest_headlines.heading: Supplementary Information
digest_headlines.headline: The supplementary figure lists case16 evidence associations and an offline re-execution that reproduced two saved tables byte for byte.

repos.title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models
repos.paper_summary: Co-Design Bench is a reference-free benchmark for coding agents that revise real users' web applications from multimodal requests. It contains 273 tasks drawn from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real coding sessions, split into Multimodal Editing (100 tasks, optional image, audio, video, or document inputs) and Repository Editing (173 tasks, coordinated multi-file changes). Each task has a runnable pre-edit app and hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria (2,331 in total). Grading is a "judge-then-refute" protocol: a fixed LLM evaluator assigns Pass, Partial, or Fail per criterion from source diffs, renders, and browser traces, then a separate LLM verifier challenges positive verdicts. Under a shared Claude Code harness, the strongest of ten endpoints (gpt-6-astra) reaches a mean strict criterion completion of 0.699 but fully completes only 26.4% of tasks. All ten endpoints score lower on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two. A limitation is that tasks evaluate a fixed request without simulated user feedback.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Co-Design Bench tests whether coding agents turn real users' multimodal revision requests into working application changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks cover screenshot reconstruction, predefined edits, and repository issues, but few cover compound revisions drawn from real coding sessions.

digest_headlines.heading: Co-Design Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Each task pairs a runnable pre-edit application with a normalized request, attachments, and hidden expert-authored criteria.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Protocol
digest_headlines.headline: A judge grades each criterion from source and browser evidence, then a separate verifier challenges positive verdicts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across ten endpoints, criterion coverage runs well ahead of complete delivery, with the top model fully passing 26.4% of tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Co-Design Bench offers a shared setting for measuring complete delivery, with runnable baselines and criterion-level evidence retained.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the WebCompass execution-regime comparison, evaluator sensitivity, resource accounting, cases, dataset composition, and evaluation details.

repos.title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right
repos.paper_summary:
Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP) is a one-line change to multi-token prediction (MTP) training that drops the residual part of the MTP cross-entropy gradient and keeps only a KL self-distillation signal toward the model's next-token prediction (NTP) distribution. The paper splits the standard MTP gradient exactly into these two parts. It recovers the KL gradient by routing gradients straight-through from the NTP cross-entropy when teacher and student share a linear output head. This avoids vocabulary-sized logit matrices and keeps fused cross-entropy kernels usable.

Soft-MTP adds no parameters and reports no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, it gives lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding, and higher zero-shot accuracy than standard MTP at every scale, and lower MTP perplexity from 689M parameters onward. At 1.2B, it improves math and code reasoning after fine-tuning. It matches or exceeds direct KL minimization on most metrics.

Limitations: the shared output head still receives cross-entropy gradients, so only the MTP heads and shared trunk get the KL signal. Sequence sharding needs a backward exchange of hidden-state gradients at shard boundaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Standard MTP training contains a residual gradient that interferes with learning, which Soft-MTP removes.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior self-distillation for MTP computes the KL explicitly or approximates it, while Soft-MTP recovers it from existing cross-entropy gradients.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Defines the next-token and multi-token cross-entropy losses for a shared linear output head.

digest_headlines.heading: Decomposing the MTP Gradient
digest_headlines.headline: The MTP cross-entropy gradient splits exactly into a KL self-distillation term and a residual term.

digest_headlines.heading: Soft Multi-Token Prediction
digest_headlines.headline: Soft-MTP sends the KL gradient through MTP heads and trunk by routing a negated residual, avoiding vocabulary-sized logits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP across 167M to 1.2B parameters on speculative decoding and downstream accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion: Practical Relevance at Frontier Scale
digest_headlines.headline: The trick needs extra communication only under sequence sharding and avoids vocabulary-sized KL tensors.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Soft-MTP is a one-line change to MTP that adds no parameters and improves NTP loss, speculative decoding and reasoning.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgements and Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The acknowledgements credit funding, inspiration from NextLat, and thanks to named collaborators.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the Soft-MTP PyTorch implementation, gradient derivations, hyperparameters, and signal-to-noise and gradient-share diagnostics.

repos.title: Solv3R: 3D Looped Transformer as a Multi-view Solver
repos.paper_summary:
Solv3R reformulates multi-view 3D reconstruction as a stationary looped transformer solver: one shared update operator is applied at every call, independent of how many calls a view has already received. It is fine-tuned from the pretrained DéjàView model, with learned constant gates replacing iteration-conditioned gates and the state rescaled to a fixed RMS norm after each update. Training uses random gradient-free solver calls, differentiable calls supervised after 24 to 48 calls, Gaussian noise or partial resets, and distillation of DéjàView outputs after 16 calls.

On the offline benchmarks in Table 1 (DTU, ETH3D, 7-Scenes, ScanNet++, nuScenes), Solv3R with 16 fixed calls reaches camera AUC@30 of 99.0 on DTU and 94.8 on ETH3D, close to DéjàView's 98.8 and 95.4. Adaptive stopping, which halts when the relative state update falls below γ = 0.02, uses 91.3 TFLOPs for 24 views, versus 75.9 for DéjàView at 16 calls. Under perturbation, Solv3R recovers accurate poses where DéjàView does not.

Limitations: the stability and correction results come from selected windows, and the stopping rule's reliability on other datasets appears only in the supplement. Solv3R's behavior beyond 64 calls is not reported in the main text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Feed-forward geometric models struggle to refine or extend reconstructions, so the paper proposes Solv3R, a reusable learned solver.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans feed-forward geometry, looped refinement and streaming reconstruction, which Solv3R applies as one solver.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A stationary learned update, trained for stability, correction and continuation, is shared across all solver calls.

digest_headlines.heading: Solver analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Solv3R's camera error stays low as updates shrink and recovers after perturbation, unlike DéjàView.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Solv3R's accuracy at 16 calls is comparable to DéjàView, and it is competitive across offline, incremental, relocalization and streaming tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues that a single learned solver can unify offline, incremental, relocalization and streaming reconstruction.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation details, evaluation protocols, extra analyses, a failure case and additional aerial and qualitative results.

repos.title: RadixFlow: Filling Execution Bubbles in Prefix-Cached Hybrid LLM Serving
repos.paper_summary: RadixFlow is a batch-construction policy for prefix-cached serving of hybrid LLMs, where a matched prefix may need recurrent state still being produced in the same round. Its state-ready traversal blocks only the consumer of that dependency, puts it in a wait queue for the next round, and keeps scanning for independent branches that fit. The paper proves that, for a fixed round and native order, the batch contains every branch that prefix-stop would select, and that no avoidable bubble remains when readiness is monotone and no other failure stops the scan. On five hybrid models, evaluated on QuALITY and RACE candidate-scoring workloads in vLLM on A800 GPUs, it lowers mean latency by 3% to 24% and worker rounds by 11% to 44% versus the native Radix scheduler, with prefix reuse within 0.03 percentage points. On the full-attention Qwen3-8B control, latency is unchanged at 16.4 s. Ablations attribute most of the gain on larger Qwen3.5 models to traversal. The authors state that evaluation covers one generated token under fixed arrival settings, and that heavier per-round cost reduces how much of the round saving reaches latency.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hybrid LLMs make a cache-matched branch wait for a same-round producer, and the native scan stalls behind it.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prefix-caching systems decide what state can be reused, while RadixFlow changes only which executable branches a round selects.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Batch construction must admit only branches with a matching prefix, usable state at the resume boundary, and fitting resources.

digest_headlines.heading: RadixFlow
digest_headlines.headline: RadixFlow blocks only the consumer of a same-round dependency and keeps scanning for independent work that fits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: RadixFlow lowers mean latency and worker rounds on the hybrid models while prefix reuse stays nearly unchanged.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A cache match is not yet a runnable branch, so schedulers should separate same-round dependencies from memory pressure.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover candidate-conditioned prefill with one generated token under frozen settings, without load sweeps or production traces.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use public benchmark inputs and public model weights, and the paper discloses assistance used in implementation and revision.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers design rationale, replay protocol, timing semantics, stream proofs, and audits of baselines and output agreement.

repos.title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
repos.paper_summary:
ChatDev is a multi-agent software development framework that uses LLM-driven agents to execute design, coding, and testing phases through structured dialogue. The system organizes work via a "chat chain," which breaks tasks into subtasks handled by pairs of agents acting as instructor and assistant. A "communicative dehallucination" mechanism reduces errors by having the assistant request specific details before generating code.

Evaluated on a dataset of 1,200 software requirements, ChatDev outperforms GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT. In Table 1, ChatDev achieves an executability score of 0.880 and a quality score of 0.395, compared to 0.415 and 0.152 for MetaGPT. Pairwise evaluations in Table 2 show ChatDev winning 77.1% of comparisons against GPT-Engineer when judged by GPT-4. Ablations in Table 4 indicate that removing agent roles drops executability from 0.880 to 0.580. Limitations include high computational costs due to multiple agents and a tendency to generate simple logic or static placeholders rather than complex database interactions, making it suitable primarily for prototypes.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev uses chat among role-playing LLM agents, with language as the shared medium, across design, coding, and testing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers LLM agents and deep learning applied to single waterfall phases, which the authors say remain isolated.

digest_headlines.heading: ChatDev
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev pairs an instructor agent and an assistant agent per subtask, linked by a chat chain and dehallucination rules.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: ChatDev scores highest on all four metrics and wins most pairwise comparisons against GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Authors conclude that language-based multi-agent communication improves software optimization and supports agent autonomy.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Agents need detailed requirements, evaluation covers limited dimensions, and multi-agent runs need more tokens and time.

repos.title: KVMem: Virtualizing Million-Token Agent Workspaces on a Consumer GPU
repos.paper_summary:
KVMem is a KV-context virtualization system that preserves overflowed agent workspace history as paged KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe. Instead of compacting older context into lossy text summaries or retrieving it as text for repeated prefill, KVMem materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model’s native context window. It uses step-level memory scheduling to update the historical working set once per agent step, query-conditioned retrieval via compact Mean-K indexes derived from the serving model’s attention space, and tiered KV management with position-consistent re-RoPE to restore selected blocks efficiently.

On LongMemEval-S, MemoryAgentBench, and AgentLongBench, KVMem generally achieves higher task utility than compaction-based approaches and reduces post-compaction recovery latency by 11.4–53.8× compared to Compact+RAG. In a DeepSWE long-context test with Qwen3.8-27B, KVMem improves task success from 43.8% to 48.4%. On a consumer laptop with a 24 GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU, KVMem supports a 1M-token virtual workspace—four times the model’s 256K-token context window—while sustaining approximately 50 tokens/s in single-session generation. Limitations include the fact that reused KV state is not mathematically equivalent to recomputing text under new contexts, and that retrieval may miss task-relevant blocks if the active execution view is too small.
